doc.title: Clyde Kerr Jr. interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rome, New York, August 22, 2006

title: Reading music, session work and adapting style at Jazz Fest stages
summary: Being a reading musician let him play sessions and several Jazz Fest stages in a day; jazz is reacting in the moment to your surroundings.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Studio work and jingles: New York session life

blocks.x: You just show up and the music’s there and you’ve got to nail it, right?

Right. You’ve got to read it. That’s what I’m saying about being a reading musician, you could react when there’s written music or I’ve done a lot of sessions where there was no music, you had to just do it from here. Or sometimes they gave you the part from the piano and you put it together. And to be able to do it all, man, means that you are able to do more things. Like in New Orleans at the Jazz and Heritage Festival back in the days when I was playing quite a bit, sometimes I’d play in Economy Hall which is the traditional jazz. Sometimes I’d go to the Ray Ban stage and that was the rhythm & blues with Dr. John and Alan Toussaint and people like that and then I’d go to the jazz tent and play my gig, play with Kidd Jordan, play with Ellis Marsalis or whatever, and then go to the funk stage and play with groups, so sometimes I would do all that in one day. And people go well how can you go from one stage to another stage playing in different styles? I say man I think it’s just like one thing to me, because everything comes from the breath and when you blow that horn, you know what your surrounding is about so you just make it go like that. So I mean if I’m playing with the Neville Brothers, I’m not going to play the same way I would play when I’m playing in Economy Hall. But it’s the same thing you know, it’s the same thing. You just make your instrument sound to blend in to the surroundings that you’re in. It’s just like going through neighborhoods in New Orleans. You know you go through different neighborhoods and you see the culture may change a little bit this and that or whatever, and you react to that. You do it automatically. Sometimes when you hang out with your friends you might speak a little bit different, use a little bit other terminology that you can’t put on tape. Or you go in the other surroundings, you react differently. So it’s all a reaction to what’s going on at the particular time. To me, and that’s what jazz is to me, you’re reacting in the moment of what is going on and what’s supposed to be happening at that particular time.
